lead: An op-amp without negative feedback has only two useful outputs: near the positive supply or near the negative supply. That makes it a comparator, a one-bit analog-to-digital block. A comparator turns a sensor voltage into a logic level. Add positive feedback and it becomes a Schmitt trigger with two thresholds, so noise cannot make the output chatter. Two comparators with an AND gate form a window detector that is high only inside a voltage band. These blocks sit in flash ADCs, thermostats, over-voltage trips, zero-crossing dimmers and counting circuits.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for saturation and the open-loop transfer curve, and Unit 4 for positive feedback and two stable states.

sections.h3: Comparator: open loop to a logic level

blocks.text: An op-amp with no negative feedback is a comparator. Its open-loop gain is very large, so a very small differential voltage drives the output to one rail. The output is +V<sub>sat</sub> or −V<sub>sat</sub>, where V<sub>sat</sub> is the saturated output magnitude, a little below the supply rail; it is not a smooth copy of the input. For an ideal comparator, v<sub>out</sub> = +V<sub>sat</sub> when v<sub>+</sub> > v<sub>−</sub>, and −V<sub>sat</sub> when v<sub>+</sub> < v<sub>−</sub>. A zero-crossing detector is the simple case with one input at 0 V: the output changes state each time the input crosses zero. The comparator converts an analog level into a logic level for a digital input, a timer or a counter.

Speed is set by propagation delay and slew rate, not by the closed-loop bandwidth of an amplifier. An open-collector or open-drain comparator needs a pull-up resistor; without it the output can sink current but cannot rise. Do not use a slow op-amp as a fast comparator without checking recovery from saturation. Stored charge in its internal nodes can delay the next edge.

sections.h3: Schmitt trigger: two thresholds from positive feedback

blocks.text: A Schmitt trigger is a comparator with positive feedback. In the inverting version, the input drives the − input. R₂ feeds the output back to the + input, and R₁ connects the + input to ground. This feedback reinforces the present state, so the circuit has two stable output states. Some syllabi call it a regenerative comparator.

With V<sub>ref</sub> = 0 V, the divider gives β = R₁/(R₁ + R₂). When the output is +V<sub>sat</sub>, the + input is at +βV<sub>sat</sub>, so the upper threshold is UTP = +βV<sub>sat</sub>. The output stays high while v<sub>in</sub> < UTP, and goes low when v<sub>in</sub> rises above UTP. When the output is −V<sub>sat</sub>, the + input is at −βV<sub>sat</sub>, so the lower threshold is LTP = −βV<sub>sat</sub>. The output stays low while v<sub>in</sub> > LTP, and goes high when v<sub>in</sub> falls below LTP. The gap is the hysteresis width W = UTP − LTP = 2βV<sub>sat</sub>.
β = R₁/(R₁ + R₂),  UTP = +βV<sub>sat</sub>,  LTP = −βV<sub>sat</sub>,  W = UTP − LTP = 2βV<sub>sat</sub>
blocks.where: β is the feedback fraction; R₁ is the resistor from the + input to ground; R₂ is the resistor from the output to the + input; V<sub>sat</sub> is the saturated output magnitude with V<sub>ref</sub> = 0 V; UTP is the upper threshold; LTP is the lower threshold; W is the hysteresis width.

blocks.text: A noisy input that wiggles by less than W cannot cause extra output transitions. The same idea cleans a slow signal in a counter or a zero-crossing detector. The non-inverting version applies the signal to the + input; its threshold algebra is different, so derive it from the node equation. For design, pick β from the required W, then choose R₁ and R₂ in the same ratio.

A window detector answers one question: is the input inside a band? Use two comparators. Comparator 1 output is high when v<sub>in</sub> > V<sub>L</sub>. Comparator 2 output is high when v<sub>in</sub> < V<sub>U</sub>. An AND gate combines their outputs. The final output is high only while V<sub>L</sub> < v<sub>in</sub> < V<sub>U</sub>; outside the band it is low. Diode logic or open-collector wired-AND can replace the gate when the comparator outputs are compatible.

This block is used as an over-voltage and under-voltage trip, a thermostat window, and a comparator bank in a flash ADC. In a lamp dimmer, a zero-crossing detector marks the AC mains crossing; the control circuit then delays the thyristor trigger. A window detector can also check that a sensor stays inside a safe range before a relay or alarm is enabled. Set V<sub>L</sub> below V<sub>U</sub>; swapping them gives no high output at all.

figure.caption: The comparator has no negative feedback; the divider returns one third of the ±11 V output to the + input, so the thresholds sit at ±3.67 V.

spec.title: Schmitt trigger with positive feedback
spec.aria: A Schmitt trigger block diagram: v_in and V_ref enter the comparator, the output saturates at ±11 V, and a divider returns β = 1/3 to the + input.

examples.question: An inverting Schmitt trigger runs on ±12 V supplies and saturates at ±11 V. The + input divider has R₁ = 10 kΩ to ground and R₂ = 20 kΩ to the output. The input drives the − input, and V_ref = 0 V. Find β, UTP, LTP and hysteresis width. A window detector on the same supplies uses V_L = 3 V and V_U = 5 V; state its high range.
steps: The divider fraction is β = R₁/(R₁ + R₂) = 10 kΩ/(10 kΩ + 20 kΩ) = 10/30 = 0.333.
With the output at +11 V, UTP = βV_sat = 0.333 × 11 V = 3.666 V ≈ 3.67 V.
With the output at −11 V, LTP = −βV_sat = −3.666 V ≈ −3.67 V.
Hysteresis width W = UTP − LTP = 3.666 V − (−3.666 V) = 7.333 V ≈ 7.33 V, also 2βV_sat = 2 × 0.333 × 11 V = 7.333 V.
The guaranteed high band is 3 V < v_in < 5 V. At exactly 3 V or 5 V the comparator sits at its switching point and the output is indeterminate in practice; treat the band edges as uncertain.
examples.answer: β ≈ 0.33, UTP ≈ +3.67 V, LTP ≈ −3.67 V, hysteresis width ≈ 7.33 V; the window output is high for 3 V < v_in < 5 V.
examples.check:
Vsat = 11.0
R1 = 10e3
R2 = 20e3
beta = R1 / (R1 + R2)
UTP = beta * Vsat
LTP = -beta * Vsat
W = UTP - LTP
VL = 3.0
VU = 5.0
print(f'{beta:.2f}')
print(f'{UTP:.2f}')
print(f'{LTP:.2f}')
print(f'{W:.2f}')
print(f'{VL:.0f}')
print(f'{VU:.0f}')

traps: Using R₂/(R₁ + R₂) instead of R₁/(R₁ + R₂) gives the wrong thresholds.
A plain comparator has no hysteresis; a slow noisy input makes the output chatter.
The saturation level is not the supply rail; use V_sat, not ±V_CC, in threshold calculations.
An open-collector comparator needs a pull-up; without it the output cannot go high.
For an inverting Schmitt trigger the input drives the − input; do not swap the UTP and LTP signs.

quiz.q: Define a comparator and state its two output levels.
quiz.a: An open-loop op-amp that outputs +V_sat when v₊ > v₋ and −V_sat when v₊ < v₋; no negative feedback.

quiz.q: Why does positive feedback give a Schmitt trigger two thresholds?
quiz.a: The output feeds back to the + input. +V_sat holds +βV_sat and −V_sat holds −βV_sat, so the switching level depends on the present state.

quiz.q: A Schmitt trigger has V_sat = ±10 V, R₁ = 20 kΩ, R₂ = 80 kΩ, V_ref = 0 V. Find β, UTP, LTP and width.
A slow input has 50 mV noise. A Schmitt trigger has W = 120 mV. What happens?
quiz.a: The noise is smaller than W, so it cannot cross both thresholds; the output has one clean transition, with no chatter.

quiz.q: When is a window detector output high?
Why does an open-collector comparator need a pull-up resistor?
quiz.a: It can only sink current; the pull-up provides the high level and sets the rise time.

quiz.q: A window detector has V_L = 1.5 V and V_U = 4.5 V. State the output for v_in = 0 V, 3 V and 5 V.
quiz.a: 0 V: low; 3 V: high; 5 V: low.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production comparators add internal hysteresis, latch enable and rail-to-rail input/output; high-speed links use them as clock slicers. Search 'comparator propagation delay', 'open-drain comparator' and 'Schmitt trigger ADC'. In modern CMOS, a dynamic comparator is common inside flash ADCs and memory sense amplifiers.
